# Introduction

A programming language is usually specified as a list of features,
and every consumer of the language — the parser, each interpreter,
the typechecker, the serialiser, the pretty-printer, every analysis —
must know all of them.  The coupling is multiplicative: each new
construct is a new obligation on every consumer, and each consumer is
a new place for two implementations of the same construct to
disagree.

The handl platform inverts that pressure twice, at two different
levels, and the inversion is the subject of this paper:

1. **The calculus is closed.**  Everything that executes is a `Term`
   in a six-combinator arrow calculus — Hughes' arrows
   [@hughes2000arrows] in the Lindley–Wadler–Yallop formulation
   [@lindley2010arrow], extended with operations and handlers in
   Sanada's style [@sanada2024arrows].  New language features do not
   add new combinators; they are expressed as combinations,
   desugarings, or normalisations of the existing set.

2. **A language is data.**  The tokens, grammar, AST shapes, eval
   schemes, type rules, and transforms that define a language are
   ordinary serializable values — fragment tables merged into a
   `Language` object — not code compiled into an engine.  Adding a
   language construct is a data change; adding a calculus combinator
   is an engine edit; the two almost never happen together.

Together these give a graded algebraic theory in the sense of
Plotkin–Power [@plotkin2003algebraic], Katsumata
[@katsumata2014parametric], and Kura [@kura2020graded]: a `Language`
is a signature, a `Term` is a term in the free arrow category over
that signature, and an execution engine is a *model* of the theory —
the Lindenbaum–Tarski reading in which syntax is data and semantics
is a choice of interpretation.  Because arrows rather than functions
are primitive, the model layer is plural by construction: tree-walk,
bytecode, and native-code engines interpret the same `Term`s, and
the type-and-law machinery interprets them again, differently.

This paper is deliberately scoped to the kernel.  It does not
describe the surface language (still unreleased), the engine
implementations (one repository per operation, `handl-lang/engine*`),
or the platform layer that composes languages, kits, and plugins
(`handl-lang/host`, whose own account belongs to the platform paper).
It describes the shared foundation those layers consume:

- @sec-calculus — the `Term` kernel: six combinators, the `Op`/`Handle`
  effect pair, and the honest accounting of the remaining auxiliary
  constructors;
- @sec-values — the `Value`/`TaggedValue` representation, including
  arrows as serializable data and nominal identity;
- @sec-language — the `Language` schema and its merge semantics;
- @sec-gmsac — the Graded Modal Sanada Arrow Calculus: grades as
  modality, operations as requests, handlers as elimination;
- @sec-morphisms — the dimension/axis structure: programs, laws, and
  higher transformations as n-morphisms of one mechanism;
- @sec-closed — why the set is closed, and the criterion for growth;
- @sec-not — what is deliberately not in the kernel.

The design claim is narrow: *a small closed calculus plus a data
schema is sufficient to host a family of languages without any engine
knowing any one of them.*  The evidence is the repository itself —
the schema, the calculus, and the law machinery are running code, and
the remaining gaps are enumerated as approximations in
@sec-status, not elided.

# The `Term` kernel {#sec-calculus}

`Term` is the arrow-calculus kernel.  It is defined once, in
`hnl-engine` (`handl-lang/engine`), and re-exported by
`handl-language` (`crates/handl-language/src/term.rs`): a `Term` is
an engine-agnostic description of *what* to evaluate, not *how*.
Engines interpret terms; the term itself is pure data — a
serde-serializable enum, versioned by `SchemeVersion` (canonical:
`"v2"`).

## The six combinators

| Combinator | `Term` variant | Constructs |
|---|---|---|
| `arr` | `Arr { dim, value }` | lift a pure value/function into an arrow |
| `>>>` (`seq`) | `Seq { axis, fst, snd }` | composition along axis `k` |
| `first` | `First { inner }` | run on the first of a pair |
| `choice` | `Choice { l, r }` | route on `Either`: left to `l`, right to `r` |
| `loop` | `Loop { body }` | feedback (trace), not iteration |
| `app` | `App { callee, args }` | higher-order arrow application |

: The closed combinator set. {#tbl-combinators}

These are the only arrow formers the kernel knows about.  With `op`
and `handle` (@sec-gmsac) they are the classical six of Hughes'
arrow interface: `arr`/`>>>` give a category, `first` gives product
structure, `choice` sum routing, `loop` a trace, and `app` the
`ArrowApply` strength that recovers monadic power — the
correspondence `ArrowApply` $\cong$ `Monad` is the central theorem of
the arrow-calculus literature [@lindley2011idioms].

The typing rules, at the theory level, are the usual ones.  Writing
$f : A \to B$ for a pure function and $a : A \rightsquigarrow B$ for
an arrow:

$$
\frac{f : A \to B}{\mathrm{arr}\,f : A \rightsquigarrow B}
\qquad
\frac{a : A \rightsquigarrow B \quad b : B \rightsquigarrow C}
     {a \mathbin{>\!\!>\!\!>} b : A \rightsquigarrow C}
$$

$$
\frac{a : A \rightsquigarrow B}
     {\mathrm{first}\;a : (A \times C) \rightsquigarrow (B \times C)}
\qquad
\frac{a : A \rightsquigarrow C \quad b : B \rightsquigarrow C}
     {\mathrm{choice}\;a\;b : (A + B) \rightsquigarrow C}
$$

$$
\frac{a : (A \times C) \rightsquigarrow (B \times C)}
     {\mathrm{loop}\;a : A \rightsquigarrow B}
\qquad
\mathrm{app} : (A \rightsquigarrow B) \times A \rightsquigarrow B
$$

Every surface construct in every language on the platform lowers to
combinations of these six — by an eval scheme declared in `Language`
data (@sec-language), not by a case in an engine.

## The effect pair: `Op` and `Handle`

Two further constructors carry the effect layer (Sanada's `op` and
`handle` [@sanada2024arrows]; @sec-gmsac develops the calculus):

- `Op { dim, name, args, source, lit }` — a named, graded operation
  request.  `source` (`ArrSource`) marks whether the request is a
  native pure op, a foreign host call (`Foreign(name)` — a
  module-registry key and capability name, *not* a dimension), a
  typecheck judgment (`Judgment`), or a dynamic host dispatch
  (`DynamicForeign`).
- `Handle { body, target, impl_ }` — scope `body` under a handler:
  `handle body with target = impl_`.  The handler is an ordinary
  arrow value, not a special construct.

## Auxiliary constructors — honest accounting

The `Term` enum in `hnl-engine` carries more than the eight forms
above, and this paper does not pretend otherwise.  The remaining
variants are data-carrying auxiliaries, not new arrow *formers* —
they add no new way to build an arrow, they move data the formers
need:

- `Const { value }` — a pure value at term level (distinct from
  `Arr`, which is a constant *arrow*);
- `Iter { fuel, predicate, step, initial }` — *bounded* iteration:
  a fuel-indexed fold used where `loop` would be unbounded;
- `Child { role }` — project the child occupying a named role of the
  current AST node (the data-driven counterpart of positional child
  access; @sec-language);
- `Src { cell }` / `Tgt { cell }` — source and target faces of a
  2-cell (@sec-morphisms);
- `Rewrite { source, target, witness }` — a witnessed rewrite step;
  the `RewriteWitness` (`Named`/`Compute`/`HandlerHint`/`Cast`)
  records *why* the step is sound;
- `RecordProj` / `RecordWith` — record field projection and update;
- `Tag { tag, value }` — tagged-value construction;
- `Cobind { grade, body }` — cobinding over a grade and body;
- `Opaque { data }` — a term in *open data form*: a tagged record
  naming a derived operator (`Path`, `Equiv`, `Whisker`, `CellId`,
  …) folded out of the closed vocabulary.  The kernel carries the
  record without structural interpretation, and `TermData::to_term`
  maps any unrecognised tag here — which is what makes the
  `Term` $\leftrightarrow$ data conversion *total*: a derived
  operator that is not (yet) spelled in the closed vocabulary still
  round-trips.

`Opaque` deserves emphasis because it is the escape hatch that keeps
the set closed in practice: an operator the surface calculus derives
(`Whisker`, `CellId`, `Univalence`) is represented as *data naming
the derivation*, not as a new enum variant.  Consumers that do not
understand the tag see an opaque record; the law machinery sees the
same record the surface forms produce.

## Dimension and axis slots are data {#sec-slots}

Two slots on the core variants make the higher-dimensional structure
of @sec-morphisms possible without new combinators:

- `Arr` and `Op` carry `dim: Box<Term>` (default `Const 1`).  A
  literal `Const n` is a numeric dimension ($\rightsquigarrow_n$); a
  literal `Const "S"` is a *named* dimension — what the graded-effect
  surface calls a grade.  One slot serves both; a grade is a named
  dimension.  Because `dim` is itself a `Term`, dimension is data
  inside the calculus, not a static annotation.
- `Seq` carries `axis: Box<Term>` (default `Const 0`).  `>>>` is
  `>>>[0]` — sequential composition of 1-cells; `>>>[k]` composes
  along the $k$-th globular axis (@sec-morphisms).

`Term::globular_dim` computes the declared dimension structurally —
the `dim` slot when it is a literal, else the greatest dimension of
the parts — and `Term::desugar` recursively expands any residual
derived forms into the core set before interpretation.

# Values {#sec-values}

The canonical value type at the `Language`/AST boundary is
`serde_json::Value` — the kernel invents no new value type there.
`handl-value` (`crates/handl-value`) provides `TaggedValue`, the
tagged representation eval engines use on hot paths, with
`From`/`Into` conversion at the boundary.  Its variants are the
calculus' needs and nothing more: `Null`, `Bool`, `Int(i64)`,
`Float`, `Str`, `Bytes`, `Arr`, `Obj`; `Pair` and
`EitherLeft`/`EitherRight` as dedicated variants (the `First`,
`Choice`, and `Loop` payload shapes); `Arrow`; `Sym` (nominal
identity); `Resource` (an RAII-wrapped opaque foreign handle); and
`Tensor` (a dense row-major `f64` carrier that engines pass through
opaquely to host functions — the `host-tensor` wire form).

## Arrows are serializable data

`TaggedValue::Arrow` is the one computational variant, and its
design is a load-bearing claim of the kernel:

> An arrow is **self-contained serializable data**: `{"__arrow__":
> true, "params": [...], "body_def": ...}` — no closures, no captured
> lexical environment, no process-local frame references.

At mint time every *free* variable in the body is substituted with
its definition-site value (`Ast::instantiate`,
`crates/handl-language/src/instantiate.rs`), so the body is a closed
term applicable without an environment.  The residual `binds` map
carries what cannot be substituted — recursion-region binders and
values that do not serialize — and `handlers` carries handlers
attached by deep-handler attach as explicit data, reinstalled on each
application.  Binder tracking during substitution is itself
data-driven over `AstShapeDef` roles (@sec-language), never
`kind ==` checks.

Two consequences follow.  First, a value can travel — across engines,
across a serialization boundary, into a cache — because nothing in it
is a pointer into a process.  Second, higher-order values need no
closure type: `call(f, x)` lowers to a pair quoted through `app`, and
an inner function referencing enclosing parameters is a bound-arrow
record — a product encoding, not an environment capture.

## Nominal identity

`TaggedValue::Sym` is a first-class nominal identity: a unique
`handle` minted from a global counter, a display `name` that is
presentation-only, and an optional single-parent `Sym` chain.
Equality is identity (`handle` equality) — two syms with equal names
are never equal — while the JSON encoding is explicit data that
round-trips the handle, so a deserialized sym compares equal to the
live sym it came from.  `Sym` is how the kernel provides nominal
objects (fresh type constructors, class-like identities) without
adding a name-generation construct to the calculus.

# Language as data {#sec-language}

The `handl-language` crate defines the schema (ADR-0044).  A
`Language` is a struct of `FragmentSet`s plus value tables — pure
serializable data end to end: no trait objects, no closures, no
`Box<dyn Behavior>`.

## The `Language` value

| Field | Type | What it declares |
|---|---|---|
| `tokens` | `FragmentSet<TokenKindDef>` | the token vocabulary and its tooling categories |
| `lexer_rules` | `FragmentSet<LexerRuleDef>` | how source text becomes tokens (`LexerPattern`s) |
| `grammar` | `FragmentSet<GrammarRow>` | how tokens become AST — binding powers, child shapes |
| `ast` | `FragmentSet<AstShapeDef>` | per node kind: payload schema, named child roles, arity, desugar |
| `eval` | `FragmentSet<EvalSchemeDef>` | how each node kind becomes a `Term` |
| `types` | `FragmentSet<TypeRuleDef>` | per node kind: `synth`/`check` `Term`s |
| `transforms` | `FragmentSet<TransformDef>` | `(pass, node_kind, priority)`-keyed rewrite/desugar rules |
| `caps` | `FragmentSet<CapabilityDecl>` | capability declarations |
| `options` | `FragmentSet<OptionSchema>` | option schemas |
| `lints`, `lsp` | `FragmentSet<…>` | lint rules; LSP surface definitions |
| `ops`, `handlers`, `handlers_by_grade` | `BTreeMap<String, Value>` | evaluated op declarations; handler values; the grade index |
| `laws`, `rewrites` | `BTreeMap<String, Value>` | declared laws and rewrite rules `source ~> target` |
| `globals` | `BTreeMap<String, Value>` | ambient global bindings seeded into engine scope |
| `scheme_version` | `SchemeVersion` | which `Term` combinator version the language targets (`"v2"`) |

: The `Language` schema (`crates/handl-language/src/language.rs`). {#tbl-language}

Two fragment rows deserve detail.  `EvalSchemeDef` is
`{id, node_kind, scheme: Term, replaces, requires}` — the eval
fragment *is* a table of `Term`s, so "how a construct executes" is a
data row an engine instantiates directly, with zero Rust arms per
construct.
`AstShapeDef` carries `children: Option<Vec<ChildRoleSpec>>` — named
roles (`role`, `variadic`, `optional`) — plus `literal_children`,
`pattern_role`, and an optional `desugar` rule that merge lowers into
the `transforms` set (a `TransformDef` under pass `"desugar"`), so a
shape and its desugaring cannot drift apart.

## Merge semantics

Composition is `Language::merge`, applied in kit-defined order.  The
policy (`FragmentSet`, `crates/handl-language/src/fragment_set.rs`)
is what makes "language as data" composable rather than merely
concatenable:

- **Override vs collision.**  A fragment declaring `replaces: [id]`
  is an explicit override: the replaced ids must be present, cyclic
  `replaces` chains are rejected, and every override is recorded in
  an auditable `override_chain`.  Two fragments targeting the same
  identity key with no `replaces` declared is a *collision* — an
  error, not a silent winner.  (`CapabilityDecl` is union/idempotent;
  `AstShapeDef` keeps the first declaration.)
- **Dependencies.**  `requires` is validated against the post-merge
  id set (`MissingRequires`).
- **Atomicity.**  `merge` operates on a clone and swaps in only on
  full success — a failed fragment commits no partial state.
- **Consistency.**  `AstShapeDef::desugar` rules are lowered into
  `transforms` at merge time; when a shape merge drops or replaces a
  declaration its synthesized `transform.desugar.*` rule is dropped
  with it, keeping the two sets in sync by construction.

Because a `Language` is a value, assembling one is ordinary
programming: the canonical eval-path fragment set is published as
YAML data in `kit-prelude-lang`, and `defining-handl`
(`crates/defining-handl`) goes further — it produces a `Language`
value describing a subset of the host language itself and evaluates
it under itself across the eval engines (the Futamura-projection
sanity check [@futamura1999partial]).

## Engines dispatch on data

The companion rule, enforced across the platform (and stated as a
rule of the kernel's own rule files):

> Dispatch on node kind via `Language` data — never a hardcoded
> `match` on kind strings.

Concretely: child positions are resolved by **named role** —
`lang.child_role_index(node.kind, "target")` for shape-level checks,
`lang.child_role_index_for(node, role)` for arity-dependent shapes
with `optional` roles, `role_name_at` for the inverse, and
`literal_child` for the literal-vs-computed distinction (ADR-0081).
Pattern-position behavior dispatches on `AstShapeDef::pattern_role`.
A language that spells `set`/`params`/`body` instead of
`assign`/`args`/`value` runs on untouched engines — AST layout
knowledge lives in the data, not in shape checks inside primitives.
What is allowed to be fixed in Rust is only the calculus vocabulary
itself: the combinator set, primitive forms, and value shapes.

The staged contract (`staged.rs`) makes the discipline precise:
`lex(lang, src)`, `parse(lang, toks)`, `eval(lang, ast)`, and
`run = eval ∘ parse ∘ lex` are typed signatures consuming only the
previous stage's output plus the `Language` spec — the crate ships
them unbound (`LangError::NotImplemented`) because engines are *not*
kernel; they are the `handl-lang/engine*` layer that binds against
these signatures.

# Grades and handlers: the GMSAC {#sec-gmsac}

The kernel's canonical execution calculus is the **Graded Modal
Sanada Arrow Calculus** — three ideas layered on the same `Term`:

1. **Arrows** — the closed set of @sec-calculus
   [@hughes2000arrows; @lindley2010arrow].
2. **Grades** — a row of algebraic capabilities annotating an arrow
   type, read as a *modality* on where the arrow may be interpreted.
3. **Sanada's handlers** — an operation request with an explicit
   continuation and a scoped interpretation of requests
   [@sanada2024arrows].

## Grade rows

A grade row is a multiset of grade terms on the arrow type:

```text
f : A ~[(Op, Query)]~> B
g : A ~[(Op, Clock, FFI)]~> B
```

`Op` is the marker grade — "this arrow is an operation request" — and
the remaining names are algebra grades: the operation is interpreted
by the innermost handler matching *any* of them.  A pure arrow has an
empty row; an `Op` adds grades; installing a handler removes one.
The row is a set, so `A ~[(Query)]~> B` sits under
`A ~[(Query, Clock)]~> B` — the usual effect-row subtyping of
Bauer–Pretnar [@bauer2014effect], restated in arrow terms.

The grade row is not decoration on top of the calculus: it *is* the
`dim` slot (@sec-slots).  The unified slot is the kernel's answer to
a question the earlier draft separated — "where do the grade bracket
and the dimension bracket live?" — they are one bracket.  A grade is
a named dimension; handler routing is dimension-typed;
`Term::dim_label` resolves the literal `Const "S"`/`Arr "S"`
positions to a routing label, and numeric literals are unnamed
dimensions.  `ArrSource::Foreign` stays strictly the host-function
boundary — a registry key, never a dimension.

In the graded-algebraic-theory reading (Katsumata's parametric effect
monads [@katsumata2014parametric], Kura's graded algebraic theories
[@kura2020graded], Sanada's category-graded theories
[@sanada2023cateff], and the category-graded monad unification of
Orchard–Wadler–Eades [@orchard2020unifying]): sorts are value
families, grades are capabilities, an operation is a graded arrow
declaration, a `Term` is a term in the free arrow category over the
signature, and a model is a `Model` — the trait in `hnl-engine` whose
`run(term, incoming, ctx)` interprets terms and whose
`rewrite(source, target, witness, ...)` interprets rewrites.
Dispatch is by grade, not by operation name: an engine seeing
`Op{name: "add"}` consults the signature for the operation's grade,
checks the carrier's declared grades, and routes to the handler for
that grade — so the same operation works on every sort that carries
it.

## Handlers as elimination

`Term::Op` and `Term::Handle` give the calculus deep, rebindable
effects.  An `Op` is a request carrying a name, arguments, and its
grade row; a `Handle` scopes a body under a handler.  The handler is
an ordinary arrow value returning a record of operation
implementations — not a special form — and installing it is the
elimination of the modal grade: bracketing a region with a handler
removes the corresponding effect from the row and restores the
previous interpretation on exit.  Runtime, `Handle` pushes its
implementation onto the `ModelCtx` handler stack and `Op` dispatch
searches it innermost-last before falling back to the value's own
grades; `Language::handlers_by_grade` is the compile-time index into
the same table, kept as data so a language's ambient handlers travel
with the language.

Because handlers are values, effect algebras are *packages*, not
kernel concepts: a resumable request algebra, a mutation algebra, a
fire-and-forget event algebra all lower to `Op`/`Handle` — the
runtime knows only the calculus and never pattern-matches on the
algebra's names.  User-space algebras are exactly Plotkin–Power
operations with Plotkin–Pretnar handlers
[@plotkin2003algebraic; @plotkin2013handling], carried on arrows per
Sanada rather than on monadic computations, and the capability view —
effects as what the context *provides* — is the Effekt line
[@brachthaeuser2020effects].

# Morphisms all the way up {#sec-morphisms}

The kernel takes one further step past "arrows compute": *everything*
is a morphism, and the same mechanism recurs up the dimensions.
This section is the theory level — the calculus structure, not a
surface syntax.

## Dimensions and axes

Writing $M[n]\langle A, B\rangle$ for the family of $n$-morphisms
between parallel $(n{-}1)$-morphisms, dimension 1 is programs and
dimension 2 is transformations between them:

```text
f, g : A ~[1]~> B            -- programs (1-morphisms between objects)
α    : f ~[2]~> g            -- a law / rewrite (2-morphism between 1-morphisms)
ω    : α ~[3]~> β            -- a transformation of laws (3-morphism)
```

Two independent indices organise the calculus.  The *dimension* $n$
in $\rightsquigarrow_n$ names what kind of cell is being built — in
`Term`, the `dim` slot of `Arr`/`Op`, which is itself a `Term` and
therefore data (@sec-slots).  The *axis* $k$ in $\mathbin{>\!\!>\!\!>}_k$
(`Seq{axis, fst, snd}`) names along which boundary cells paste:
$>>>[0]$ pairs cells across composition of their boundary morphisms,
$>>>[1]$ stacks them along the morphism direction, and the boundary
law is globular — $\mathrm{tgt}_k(a) = \mathrm{src}_k(b)$, enforced
wherever `>>>[k]` executes.  `Term::globular_dim` gates $k < n$: the
value model currently carries a single cell shape at dimension 2, so
axes 0 and 1 execute meaningfully and $k \geq 2$ is a dimension error
for ordinary operands — an implementation boundary, stated honestly,
not a metatheorem.

The resulting structure is a *weak globular* presentation: higher
laws are genuine higher cells (proof-relevant), not strict
equalities, with the strict fragment kept as a fast path (below).
Cubical Kan structure is deliberately deferred — it would arrive as
a cube-diagram fragment over the same `Term`s, not a rewrite of the
directed calculus.  For the $n$-categorical background see Leinster's
survey [@leinster2002ncat].

## Laws are 2-morphisms — and therefore data

The structural laws of the calculus are not declarations in a
separate rule language; they are 2-morphisms:

```text
rightUnit : (f >>> id) ~[2]~> f
assoc     : ((f >>> g) >>> h) ~[2]~> (f >>> (g >>> h))
```

An inhabitant of $M[2]$ is simultaneously a rewrite rule, a proof,
and a program transformation; the intended reading is supplied by the
consumer — an eval engine, the law machinery, or a rewrite engine —
not by a syntactic distinction in the calculus.  `Src`/`Tgt` project
the boundary faces of a cell; `Rewrite{source, target, witness}`
carries a witnessed step; and derived cell operators (`CellId`,
`Whisker`, horizontal/vertical cell composition) fold to `Opaque`
tagged records when they are not spelled by a `Seq{axis}` scheme.
`Language::laws` and `Language::rewrites` are the value tables these
live in — again, data.

Two modules in `handl-language` are the law machinery over this IR:

- `law_inference` — normalizes `Term` graphs to a fixpoint under the
  CutElim-derived rewrites (`Seq(id,G) ⇒ G`, `Seq(G,id) ⇒ G`,
  `Seq(First G, First H) ⇒ First(Seq G H)`, `First id ⇒ id`) and
  decides law equality by comparing normal forms — `law_equal`, with
  `infer_laws` matching a scheme against a catalog of structural law
  patterns.  Its scope is honestly bounded: inference works only for
  the CutElim-proven structural fragment (the `First` functor laws);
  semantic laws require explicit axioms, and the module documents
  that boundary rather than blurring it.
- `quantified_laws` — explicit `forall f g. lhs = rhs` quantified law
  syntax over `Term`s, checked by instantiation under a
  representative substitution set: a heuristic strong for
  schema-level laws, not a completeness proof — the mechanized proof
  lives in the research prototype's Lean development
  [@handl2026kernelpoc].

`dynamic_handlers` completes the trio: runtime verification of
handler implementations against declared laws
(`verify_at_runtime`, `VerifiedImplStore`, `dynamic_dispatch`) — the
correspondence between unhandled operations and effect rows
[@bauer2014effect] checked where it can be checked, at runtime.

This is the sense in which the kernel subsumes what other systems
keep as four subsystems — a program IR, a rule language, a proof
syntax, and a metaprogramming facility: here they are $M[1]$,
$M[2]$, $M[2]$, and $M[{\geq}3]$ of one mechanism.  The same point is
what makes the kernel a natural substrate for the org's
equality-saturation and discovery work — laws and rewrites are values
in the same calculus the engines execute, so a rule bank is data and
a derivation is a replayable witness [@tate2009; @willsey2021egg;
@eqsat2026substrate].

# Why the set is closed {#sec-closed}

The six combinators (plus `Op`/`Handle`) are the *only* arrow formers
the kernel knows, and the closure is a design choice, not an
oversight.

## The cost of an open kernel

An open kernel — one where each feature introduces a combinator —
accumulates special cases: every combinator must be understood by
every consumer of `Term` — each interpreter, the typechecker, the law
machinery, the serialiser, the pretty-printer, every handler that
interprets a program.  Each new combinator multiplies the surface
those consumers must cover, and each is a new place for them to
disagree.  The closed kernel pays the cost of a new feature once, at
the boundary where it is translated into the calculus — not in every
consumer downstream.

## Minimality evidence

Closure is only defensible if the set is also *minimal* — otherwise a
dropped combinator is a latent hole, not a design.  The research
prototype that precedes this kernel
[@handl2026kernelpoc] investigated exactly that: at the arrow-graph
level the primitive set is *independent* — none of `arr` /
composition / `first` / sum routing / `loop` is derivable from the
others — and the independence and classification results are
mechanized in Lean 4 (the free-arrow generator argument: e.g. no
generator can produce `Sum`/`Prod` output from the wrong primitives;
`loop` is independent in a total setting).  The sixth combinator,
`app`, is not redundant either: it is precisely the strength that
makes `ArrowApply` $\cong$ `Monad`
[@lindley2011idioms] — the freer-arrow insight that explicit
higher-order application recovers the structure opaque continuations
lose [@kiselyov2015freer; @vandomelen2025freer].

## How features enter without new combinators

A new construct enters at one of three boundaries, none of which
touches the kernel:

1. **Desugaring** — the grammar/`ast` fragments declare a shape whose
   `desugar` rule or `eval` scheme lowers the construct to existing
   `Term`s before the kernel ever sees it.  Cheapest; the kernel is
   unaware.
2. **Normalisation** — a transform pass eliminates the construct's
   encoding between lowering and interpretation.  The module system
   is the worked example in the platform: imports and exports are
   encoded as ordinary `Op`s and then inlined away, so the kernel
   never learns that modules existed.
3. **Handler interpretation** — the construct is an `Op` whose
   meaning a handler supplies.  The kernel carries the request
   opaquely; a `Model` that does not understand it refuses to
   interpret it — which is *correct*, because interpretation is a
   model-level fact.

And when even a *scheme* is the wrong level — a derived operator like
`Whisker` or `Path` — `Opaque` carries it as data naming the
derivation (@sec-calculus).

## When the set should grow

Closed is not frozen.  A seventh combinator is justified only when a
feature cannot be expressed as a combination of the existing set
without losing a property every consumer relies on — that the graph
is finite, that feedback is well-founded, that terms serialize.  Such
cases are rare and belong to an ADR.  The default answer is no: find
a combination, a desugaring, or a normalisation.

# What the kernel is not {#sec-not}

The kernel's power is what it excludes.  Explicitly:

- **Not a language.**  There is no user syntax anywhere in the
  kernel: tokens, grammar, and AST shapes are `Language` data.
  (`Term` constructors are the calculus vocabulary, not a syntax.)
- **Not an engine.**  `lex`/`parse`/`eval` exist only as staged
  signatures returning `NotImplemented`; every interpreter lives in
  the `handl-lang/engine*` repos and binds the `Model`/`ModelData`
  traits.
- **No modules, imports, or files.**  These are source-level concerns
  normalised away before the kernel; `ArrSource::Foreign` is a
  registry *key*, not a module system.
- **No rules language.**  Laws and rewrites are `Term`s at dimension
  2 stored in `Language::laws`/`rewrites` — not a parallel DSL.
- **No closures or environments.**  Arrow values are self-contained
  serializable data (@sec-values); `instantiate` eliminates free
  variables at mint.
- **No concrete effect algebras.**  Query/command/event-style
  algebras are package data lowering to `Op`/`Handle`; the kernel
  dispatches on grade rows only.
- **No concrete type system.**  `types` is a fragment set of
  `synth`/`check` `Term`s; what counts as a type is a `Model` choice.
- **No host composition.**  `Plugin`/`Host`/`Operation`/`Behavior`/
  `RuleAcceptor`/`Contribution`, kits, manifests, and option
  resolution are the platform layer (`handl-lang/host`), cited here
  only as the consumer.
- **No extension protocol details.**  `handl-ext` provides the shared
  ABI — JSON over a C boundary: `handl_ext_manifest`,
  `handl_ext_dispatch`, `handl_ext_free` — so hosts and extensions
  evolve independently; who loads what is a platform concern.
- **No serialization of authority.**  A `Resource`/`Foreign` value
  crosses the boundary opaquely; capability tracking is platform
  policy, not kernel semantics.

# Implementation status {#sec-status}

The kernel is `handl-lang/kernel`, a cargo workspace:

| Crate | Contents |
|---|---|
| `handl-language` | the `Language` schema, `FragmentSet` merge, the `Ast` arena, `staged` dispatch signatures, `law_inference`, `quantified_laws`, `dynamic_handlers`, `instantiate`, `capabilities`, `token_classes`, `verdict`, `version` — plus the `Term`/`ArrSource`/`RewriteWitness` re-export from `hnl-engine` |
| `handl-value` | `TaggedValue`, `Sym`, `TensorValue`, `ForeignResource`, JSON (`serde_json::Value`) conversions |
| `handl-ext` | the extension ABI (`ExtensionManifest`, `ExtRequest`, `ExtResponse`, `export!`, discovery/loading) |
| `defining-handl` | self-hosting infrastructure: a `Language` value describing the language subset, plus the self-hosting corpus |
| floor-library crates (`bytes`, `cmp`, `combinators`, `error`, `mood`, `obj`, `ops`, `prim`, `prim-handl`, `type`) | substrate packages providing the base op/grade tables |
| `hnl-engine` (dep, `handl-lang/engine`) | `Term`, `TermData`, `Model`, `ModelData`, `ModelCtx`, `CompositeModel`, `AstView`/`LanguageView` |

: Kernel workspace map. {#tbl-crates}

What is *proven* by the tree: a `Language` value can describe a
language and be evaluated under itself — `defining-handl`'s corpus
runs across the platform's eval engines, and the Futamura-projection
path (compiling the language-as-data interpreter) is exercised
[@futamura1999partial].  What is deferred — full self-hosting of the
entire surface language, and a standalone-binary bootstrap — is
documented in the crate's own honesty note.

Documented approximations (implementation debt, not design gaps),
condensed from the working draft [@handl2026kernelpoc]:

- The value model carries one cell shape at dimension 2, so `>>>[k]`
  executes for $k \in \{0, 1\}$; generalising past 2-cells is open.
- Only literal axes and dimensions resolve; a non-literal axis falls
  back with a warning rather than evaluating a computed boundary.
- `cell_boundary`-style projection assumes globularity (the globe
  condition is assumed, not verified).
- Quantified-law checking is substitution-tested, not complete
  (@sec-morphisms).
- A composite of dependent operands flattens to a plain function
  type at composition — dependent-aware unification exists but a
  composed body cannot carry its closure across `>>>`.

# Related work

**Arrows.**  Hughes introduced arrows as a generalisation of monads
[@hughes2000arrows]; Lindley, Wadler, and Yallop gave the arrow
calculus its minimal form and the idiom/arrow/monad correspondence
[@lindley2010arrow; @lindley2011idioms].  Our `Term` is that calculus
realised as *data* — serializable, dispatched on, rewritten — rather
than as a language's type class.

**Effects on arrows.**  Lindley first extended algebraic effects and
handlers to idioms and arrows [@lindley2014algebraic]; Sanada gave
the arrow calculus operations and handlers with operational and
denotational semantics [@sanada2024arrows] and the category-graded
theory behind the grade-as-morphism reading [@sanada2023cateff].
The generic algebraic-effects line — Plotkin–Power operations
[@plotkin2003algebraic], Plotkin–Pretnar handlers
[@plotkin2013handling], the Bauer–Pretnar effect system
[@bauer2014effect], and capability-style effect polymorphism
[@brachthaeuser2020effects] — is the row-and-handler semantics the
GMSAC restates on arrows; Moggi's monadic metalanguage
[@moggi1991notions] is the ancestor everything here descends from.

**Grades and indexing.**  Katsumata's parametric effect monads
[@katsumata2014parametric], Atkey's parameterised notions of
computation [@atkey2009parameterised], Kura's graded algebraic
theories [@kura2020graded], and the category-graded unification
[@orchard2020unifying] cover the "grade is data about the
computation" axis; the kernel's `dim`-as-`Term` pushes it one step
further — the index itself is a term of the calculus.

**Explicit vs opaque effects.**  Kiselyov's freer monads
[@kiselyov2015freer] made continuations inspectable data; freer
arrows [@vandomelen2025freer] confirm that the explicit input
parameter is what keeps fanout and choice *semantically* expressible —
the analysis the `Op`-as-request design relies on.

**Language as data.**  The claim that a theory's terms, taken modulo
its laws, are themselves an algebraic object is Lindenbaum–Tarski's;
Lawvere's functorial semantics made "theory as data, model as
functor" precise [@lawvere1963functorial].  Equality saturation
[@tate2009; @willsey2021egg] is the adjacent machinery for which
laws-as-data is load-bearing — the org's `eqsat` substrate consumes
exactly this kernel [@eqsat2026substrate].  The higher-categorical
backdrop for the dimension story is standard
[@leinster2002ncat]; the Futamura reading of language-as-data is
Futamura's [@futamura1999partial].

**Within the org.**  The research prototype (`host/research/arrow-
calculus-kernel-poc`) carried the mechanized minimality results and
the working paper draft this paper tightens [@handl2026kernelpoc];
the architecture decisions live in the host repo's ADR series —
ADR-0044 (language as data), ADR-0052/0104b (the `Term` kernel),
ADR-0076/0098 (handlers and grades), ADR-0081 (AST roles),
ADR-0103/0106/0119–0120 (opaque data forms, the object/arrow world,
the unified dimension slot) [@handl2026adrs].

# Limitations and open questions

- **Metatheory is ahead of the machine where the machine is honest
  about it.**  Whether $M[n]$ as implemented is a family of
  categories, which coherence laws hold between axes, and which
  dimension expressions are statically normalizable are open;
  interchange and higher unitor/associator structure are not yet
  inhabited cells.
- **The globular boundary is enforced, not verified.**  Globularity
  is assumed where cells are built (@sec-status); the value model
  caps pasting at dimension 2.
- **Law inference is a strict fast path.**  It covers the
  CutElim-proven structural fragment only; general law equality is
  not decidable here, and quantified-law checking is a heuristic.
- **Dependence is structural, not yet eliminative.**  Families
  indexed by higher cells and dependent elimination (refining a
  scrutinee's index per match arm) need an equality type the kernel
  deliberately does not carry.
- **The operational semantics' dimensional lift is partial.**  `Op`/
  `Handle` ride the unified dimension slot, but how Sanada's
  semantics lift through arbitrary dimensions is open.
- **Self-hosting is mechanism, not completion** — a subset corpus,
  not the whole surface language (@sec-status).

The claim that survives these limitations is the one this paper set
out to check: computation and reasoning about computation — programs,
laws, handlers, and the languages that produce all three — are
expressible in *one* closed calculus, whose consumers are models and
whose languages are data.
